structure.title: Institutional Background (U.S. income tax, IRS audits, EITC)
Empirical Framework (race imputation and disparity estimators)
Race Estimate Calibration and Statistical Bias Assessment
Algorithmic Bias in Refundable Credit Prediction (VII.C)
Supplementary Material and Data Availability Statement
References (final extracted page is an unrelated publisher insert)

observations.statement: The paper formally defines the audit disparity as the population difference in audit rates between the (unobserved) protected group and its complement, and states that estimating this parameter is the central empirical objective.

The race-imputation step relies on an explicit conditional-independence assumption, that name and geography are independent given race, which the authors write out formally and flag as a known, likely-violated simplification.

The paper names and formally contrasts two disparity estimators, a probability-weighted estimator and a linear-regression estimator, deriving closed-form conditions under which each is upward- or downward-biased for the true disparity.

The authors state the covariate-independence conditions each estimator needs to be valid and explain concretely what real-world channel, such as unmeasured differences in household structure, would violate each condition.

When the sign conditions needed to rank the two estimators hold, the paper interprets the pair jointly as a partial-identification bounds approach, reporting them as lower and upper bounds on the true disparity rather than as competing point estimates.

The core analysis uses comprehensive, confidential administrative tax-return microdata for a full national filing population in a single primary tax year, supplemented by IRS audit-outcome records linked to those returns.

The primary results focus on one tax year chosen because audit outcomes were most fully resolved at analysis time, while the authors also pool several additional years of randomly sampled research-audit data for precision and check that patterns hold across a wider multi-year window.
observations.locator: Section IV.A; robustness across years discussion

observations.statement: Data-linkage and validation steps that required nonanonymized taxpayer identifiers were carried out by government economists in a separate, controlled environment, with only anonymized results passed to the rest of the research team.

To obtain ground-truth race information for validation, the authors match tax records to publicly available state voter-registration records using name and address, and reweight the resulting linked sample to better resemble the national filing population for some calibration exercises.

A subset of taxpayers lack one or more inputs needed to impute race; rather than dropping them, the main analysis imputes race from the available subset of attributes, and a separate robustness column re-estimates the disparity after excluding this subgroup entirely.
The audit outcome is a binary indicator for whether a filed return was ever selected for an operational or research audit, measured as of a fixed multi-year completion cutoff rather than at filing.

The key explanatory variable is not observed race but an estimated probability that the primary filer is Black, built from a naive-Bayes combination of first name, surname, and census block-group racial composition.

Underreporting is defined as the gap between a taxpayer's correct tax liability and the amount reported, estimated from adjustments detected in intensive random research audits, and is later split into the portion attributable to overclaimed refundable credits versus other sources.
Dollar-denominated quantities drawn from research audits conducted in earlier years are converted to a common price basis so they are comparable with the primary study year.

The main disparity table reports the probability-weighted and linear estimators as separate rows within panels defined by population (overall, EITC claimants, nonclaimants) and by audit subtype (timing, correspondence versus field), with a companion row for the mean audit rate and the number of returns per panel.

The table notes state that reported standard errors come from the asymptotic distributions of the disparity estimators derived analytically in the online appendix, rather than from a conventional clustered or heteroskedasticity-robust regression command.

Because the design is a bounds/disparity estimator rather than a panel regression, none of the reported specifications include fixed effects; subgroup and audit-type breakdowns are instead reported as separate table panels and columns.

For the headline disparity table, precision is reported using standard errors from a formula for the asymptotic sampling distribution of the probability-weighted and linear estimators, developed in the online appendix, rather than a clustering argument.
observations.locator: Table I notes; online appendix reference

observations.statement: For several figures, uncertainty is instead summarized with confidence intervals built from a bootstrap procedure that repeatedly resamples the underlying estimation data, distinct from the closed-form asymptotic approach used in the main disparity table.

The authors note their headline confidence interval reflects only sampling uncertainty in outcomes and abstracts from uncertainty in the race-probability estimates, and report as a check that a cited dual-bootstrap procedure accounting for both sources yields somewhat less precise estimates.

A calibration exercise compares estimated race probabilities against self-reported race in the matched validation sample, checking whether predicted probabilities track the 45-degree line, and repeats the check separately for EITC claimants and nonclaimants.

A formal test of the sign of the key bias-determining covariance terms from the paper's bias proposition is reported, estimated separately by race and by predicted-race percentile and aggregated by population share, rejecting a one-sided null in the hypothesized direction.
observations.locator: Section V.B; results tabulated in the online appendix

observations.statement: As a diagnostic on whether observed underreporting differences alone explain the disparity, the authors construct an infeasible oracle selection rule ranking returns by true underreporting and compare the disparity it would induce against the status quo across a range of hypothetical audit rates.

To assess whether the single-state validation sample generalizes, the authors match to voter records in several additional states and report that the sign of the key covariance terms is stable, while noting the additional matches use a more recent voter-file year and a lower match rate.

A robustness table varies the approach to race imputation, including dropping observations missing input variables, relaxing the naive-Bayes independence assumption with an alternative sampling procedure, recalibrating probabilities against the validation sample, and imputing race from geography alone, reporting that headline results are qualitatively unchanged.
observations.locator: Online Appendix Table A.12, discussed in main text

observations.statement: The authors repeat the headline disparity estimation for several additional tax years beyond the primary study year and report that the pattern is comparable across years, summarized in appendix figures rather than a main-text table.

As a robustness check on the counterfactual audit-selection results, the authors reconstruct the algorithm comparison holding fixed the share of audits directed at higher-cost business-income issues, and separately using a more conservative measure of per-audit examiner cost, reporting the qualitative pattern is unchanged under both variants.

The authors cross-check the closed-form probability-weighted and linear disparity estimates against bounds computed by a linear program that optimizes directly over distributions consistent with the assumptions of their bias proposition, reporting comparable results between the two approaches.

Disparities are broken out by marital status, filer gender, and dependent-claiming status among EITC claimants, with the subgroup splits presented as illustrating where the disparity is concentrated rather than as a prespecified heterogeneity analysis.

Audit rates by race are also reported within deciles of the underreporting distribution constructed from random research-audit data, letting the authors check whether the racial gap persists after conditioning on a taxpayer's true underreporting level.

The paper interprets its unconditional audit-rate disparity by benchmarking it against the overall population audit rate to express the gap in both relative and absolute terms, and situates the finding relative to prior suggestive evidence on regional and county-level audit patterns by race.

The authors translate a hypothetical shift in the audit-selection objective into operational terms by comparing the resulting change in per-return examination cost against the resulting change in detected underreporting, framing it as a rough cost-effectiveness check rather than a full optimal-policy calculation.

The authors state explicitly that their analysis is limited to disparities affecting Black taxpayers and does not address other racial or ethnic groups, flagging this as an important omission for future work.

The conclusion notes that for higher-income taxpayers, whose audit selection may not be fully automated, the authors cannot rule out disparate treatment as a contributing channel, distinguishing this from the EITC population where selection is described as automated and race-blind.

The paper cautions that its counterfactual audit-algorithm analysis does not incorporate the full set of operational constraints facing the tax authority, such as which issues suit correspondence versus in-person audit, and that a complete optimal-policy analysis would need to account for these factors.

Several figures use binned scatterplots, grouping taxpayers into equal-sized bins by predicted race probability or income and plotting mean outcomes per bin with confidence bands, rather than showing raw microdata points.

Figure and table notes routinely specify which estimator (probability-weighted or linear) generated the reported quantity, the population underlying the panel, and how displayed intervals or standard errors were constructed, so estimator choice is traceable from the notes alone.
observations.locator: Notes to Figures III, VII, VIII

observations.statement: Rather than a single general-purpose summary statistics table, the paper distributes descriptive detail for its audited-return population across several purpose-built tables that pair estimated disparities with return characteristics under each counterfactual algorithm.
The disparity tables and figures report point estimates with standard errors or confidence intervals rather than using significance-star notation.

The paper includes a formal data-availability statement pointing to a public replication archive hosted on an institutional data repository, described as containing the code that replicates the paper's tables and figures.
observations.quote: Code replicating the tables and figures

observations.statement: The same statement implicitly distinguishes the replication code, which is shared, from the underlying confidential administrative tax data, which is not described as being made available.

The introduction closes with an explicit roadmap paragraph mapping each numbered section to its topic, from institutional background through the empirical strategy, data, calibration results, disparity results, and mechanism analysis.

The introduction previews the paper's main findings in an explicit ordinal sequence before the corresponding sections are presented, including the headline disparity finding, the EITC-driven concentration of the disparity, and the algorithmic-objective mechanism.

Following the results preview, the introduction sets out the paper's contributions in distinct paragraphs: a substantive contribution to the tax-and-race literature, a methodological contribution on partial identification with an unobserved protected class, and a connection to the algorithmic-fairness literature on outcome choice.

The paper structures its empirical sections so headline disparity estimates come first, robustness checks for the race-imputation approach are presented immediately after as their own subsection, and the investigation of underlying mechanisms follows in a separate, later section.

Mechanism evidence is built by simulating alternative audit-selection algorithms that vary only the ranking objective, total underreporting versus refundable-credit overclaims, while holding the audit rate fixed, and comparing the racial composition each counterfactual algorithm would select.

To explain why the algorithmic objective matters, the authors compare the prevalence of specific error types, dependent-eligibility errors versus business-income underreporting, by race, describing the resulting explanation as consistent with rather than definitively proving the underlying mechanism.

Beyond the algorithmic-objective channel, the authors state they separately checked and found no evidence that the disparity is driven by racial differences in reported income, household composition, or tax-preparer use, explicitly labeling part of this supplementary analysis as suggestive rather than conclusive.

Validation of the race-imputation approach relies primarily on matched records from a single state, and the authors treat that state's data as the main calibration source while using other states only as a supporting check.

In the conclusion, the authors distinguish causes of the disparity that tax-authority administrators could address through algorithm redesign from causes rooted in externally set rules, such as congressionally defined credit-eligibility criteria and agency funding levels, to clarify the scope of policy levers their results speak to.

The tax and audit data underlying the analysis are described as confidential administrative records obtained through the authors' institutional affiliations with the tax authority and Treasury, rather than collected by the research team or purchased commercially.

Race information is not directly available in the tax data and is instead produced by linking or combining several external administrative and survey-derived sources, including mortgage-application records, decennial census surname files, and community survey estimates, to build the race-imputation model.

concordance.paper_says: Reports probability-weighted and linear closed-form disparity estimators as the paper's headline estimator, evaluated directly from taxpayer-level audit outcomes and estimated race probabilities.
concordance.card_shows: Records four modeling specs (s1 RandomForestRegressor, s2 RandomForestClassifier, s3 smf.wls decomposition, s4 linprog); none corresponds to the closed-form weighted-average/regression-on-b disparity estimator described as the paper's main estimator.

concordance.paper_says: Trains a random forest regression model on randomly sampled audit data to predict a taxpayer's dollar underreporting from features available to selection algorithms.

A footnote describes an alternative classification-style model trained to predict the probability of overclaiming a refundable credit, contrasted with the regression-style model used in the main results.

Formally decomposes the overall audit disparity into additive components (within-EITC-claimant, within-nonclaimant, and EITC-claiming-rate terms) using group-specific audit rates and claim probabilities.
concordance.card_shows: s3: smf.wls weighted least squares regression with HC1 covariance, method=decomposition, fe=None.

concordance.paper_says: Main text does not describe the decomposition's standard errors as coming from a weighted-least-squares regression with heteroskedasticity-robust covariance; inference for the headline table is instead attributed to closed-form asymptotic formulas or bootstrap resampling.
concordance.card_shows: s3 code explicitly requests cov_type='HC1' (heteroskedasticity-robust) standard errors.

concordance.paper_says: Cross-checks the closed-form disparity bounds against a linear program that directly solves for the maximum and minimum disparity values consistent with the paper's bias-sign assumptions.
The design is a cross-sectional disparity/bounds estimator and a set of counterfactual selection simulations; no panel or regression fixed effects are mentioned anywhere in the empirical strategy.
concordance.card_shows: All four recorded specs (s1-s4) show fe=None.

concordance.paper_says: Standard errors for the headline table come from an asymptotic-distribution formula for the disparity estimators, and confidence intervals elsewhere come from resampling; no cluster level is named anywhere in the main text.
concordance.card_shows: Recorded se fields for s1-s3 are 'robust/None' or 'None/None', with no cluster_level populated for any spec.

concordance.paper_says: The comparison group is explicitly Black versus non-Black taxpayers, and within that, EITC claimants versus nonclaimants, defined from the estimated race probability.
concordance.card_shows: The printed design records (d1-d4) carry no comparison_group field.

concordance.paper_says: The sample is the full national filing population for a primary study year, with the counterfactual-algorithm exercises restricted to EITC claimants in the pooled random research-audit sample.
concordance.card_shows: The printed design records do not surface a sample-restriction field distinguishing the full population from the EITC/NRP-restricted subsample used in the mechanisms section.

concordance.paper_says: The main text only states that additional detail on the predictive model is provided in an online appendix, without describing a cross-validation or train/test procedure in the main text.
concordance.card_shows: diag x1 tagged multiple_testing, described as '5 cross-validation folds with train/test split via KFold'.

concordance.paper_says: Reports a dual-bootstrap procedure, citing an external methodology paper, that resamples both over the estimated race-probability posteriors and over the taxpayer sample to capture an additional source of estimation uncertainty.
concordance.card_shows: diag x2 tagged pretrend_test, described as a dual bootstrap procedure bootstrapping over BIFSG posteriors and over taxpayers.
concordance.note: the card's automatic 'pretrend_test' tag is a mislabel; the underlying procedure matches the paper's stated dual-bootstrap uncertainty check rather than a difference-in-differences pre-trend test.

concordance.paper_says: Presents numbered main-text tables and numbered main-text figures, each with detailed notes describing its construction.
concordance.card_shows: The card's --specs summary reports zero recorded tables and zero recorded figures.

concordance.paper_says: Explicitly names its data sources as confidential IRS administrative microdata, IRS audit records, and several external race-imputation inputs, plus a public Harvard Dataverse replication archive.
concordance.card_shows: The printed card summary lists only software packages (sklearn, statsmodels, scipy) and no data_source field.

gaps: No explicit preregistration, pre-analysis plan, or IRB/ethics statement appears in the main text; the paper analyzes existing confidential administrative government data rather than a designed experiment, so a preregistration statement may not be expected.

The Online Appendix, referenced repeatedly for proofs, additional tables (A.1-A.25 range), and extended robustness or mechanism detail, is a separate document hosted by the journal and is not part of the supplied text; its content could not be read directly and observations about it are paraphrases of what the main text says the appendix contains.

No explicit clustering-level justification (choice of cluster variable) is stated anywhere in the main text; inference instead relies on estimator-specific asymptotic-distribution formulas and bootstrap resampling, so the standard `cluster_at_*` tags do not apply.
The main text does not itself state which software packages or versions were used to fit the random forest or linear-program models; that detail is only visible in the replication code.

No placebo-cutoff or placebo-outcome diagnostic in the regression-discontinuity or event-study sense is used, consistent with the paper's design being a partial-identification bounds and counterfactual-simulation approach rather than a discontinuity or staggered-adoption design.

reading.note: Read the entire extracted text linearly from the title and abstract through the reference list in five sequential chunks (lines 1-620, 621-1240, 1241-1860, 1861-2480, 2481-2512), covering pages 1-52 of the text file. The paper's Online Appendix (proofs, additional tables, and extended robustness/mechanism detail cited throughout) is hosted separately by the journal and is not included in this text file, so it could not be read directly. The final extracted page is an unrelated Northwestern University prize announcement inserted by the publisher, not part of the article itself.
